also.hook: Clement Delangue co-founded Hugging Face in 2016 with Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, originally as a chatbot app, and steered it into the default home for sharing open-source AI models and datasets. Before that he worked in product management at Moodstocks, a computer vision startup that Google acquired the same year Hugging Face began. As CEO he built a platform that by September 2026 hosted more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets used by more than 18 million developers. That same month he agreed to sell the company to Nvidia for roughly 12.9 billion dollars, negotiating to keep Hugging Face open across clouds, frameworks and chip vendors rather than tied to Nvidia's hardware alone.
also.name: Clement Delangue

also.hook: François Chollet created Keras, the deep learning library that became a default entry point into neural networks for millions of developers, while working as a Google engineer for close to a decade. In 2019 he published the ARC-AGI benchmark, arguing that measuring intelligence required tasks a system could not memorize its way through, and in 2024 he put a million dollars behind a public prize to beat it. He left Google in November 2024 to co-found Ndea with former Zapier president Mike Knoop, betting that program synthesis rather than further scaling is the more promising path toward general AI systems.
also.name: François Chollet

also.hook: Julien Chaumond co-founded Hugging Face in 2016 and has served as its chief technology officer since, building the technical infrastructure, the Hub, the Transformers library, and the huggingface_hub client, that turned the company into the default distribution point for open machine learning models. Before Hugging Face he ran two earlier startups, Prodcast and the reading platform Glose, and advised the French Deputy Minister for Digital Affairs. He describes Hugging Face's approach as belonging to its user community rather than standing apart from it, a framing that has shaped the company's open-source strategy as its Hub scaled to millions of hosted models and datasets.
also.name: Julien Chaumond
also.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Hugging Face

also.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.
also.name: Tim O'Reilly
also.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement

name: Open Source Maintainers
blurb:
This section is meant to profile the maintainers of critical open-source AI infrastructure, the people whose unpaid or under-resourced work keeps widely depended-on projects running. In its current state it is effectively a placeholder rather than a populated roster.

The page is regenerated by the same daily pipeline as the rest of the ecosystem section, most recently on September 5, 2026, but the maintainer roster itself is built through editorial research as profiles are written, not from an automated feed. That means growth here depends on manual research capacity rather than a live data source, and coverage will stay thin until more profiles are added.

As it stands, the section holds exactly one entry, and that entry is not a maintainer profile at all. It is Tim O'Reilly, the publisher credited with naming both the open source movement and Web 2.0, included here as an adjacent figure rather than someone who maintains a specific codebase today. Zero dedicated maintainer profiles have been completed. Readers should not expect to find coverage yet of the maintainers behind major frameworks or widely used libraries. This is one of the least developed sections of the observatory, and its current content reflects an early stage of building the roster rather than a judgment about who matters most in open-source AI maintenance work. A useful next addition would be profiles of the maintainers behind widely depended-on single-maintainer projects, the kind of dependency the 2024 XZ Utils backdoor made visible, where the security of a large share of downstream software rested on one person volunteering unpaid time.

reading.body:
This category profiles one person, Tim O'Reilly, credited here with coining both open source and Web 2.0 at conferences he convened, alongside a publishing house the data describes as a technical-literacy backbone for programmers.

That the entire Open Source Maintainers category currently holds a single profile, and that the profile is a publisher and conference convener rather than a code contributor, is worth noting on its own terms. The data frames O'Reilly's pattern as recognizing a technology shift before the industry had language for it and then naming it, a description of influence through terminology and publishing rather than through maintaining a specific codebase.

With one entry and no metrics attached, this page cannot speak to how many open-source maintainers the AI ecosystem depends on or what work they do day to day. It documents one person's role in naming movements that the AI infrastructure this site tracks, open source software chief among them, now runs on.

profiles.hook: Georgi Gerganov changed how large language models reach ordinary computers. Working from Sofia, Bulgaria, he built the ggml tensor library and then llama.cpp, a C and C++ inference engine that let Meta's LLaMA models run on a laptop through aggressive quantization instead of a data-center GPU. He founded ggml.ai in 2023 on pre-seed funding from Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross to sustain the project, and in February 2026 he and his team joined Hugging Face so llama.cpp would have long-term backing while staying fully open source.
profiles.name: Georgi Gerganov

quote.text: 65 billion parameters, you probably need about 40 gigs of RAM, with 4-bit quantization. So this can run on a MacBook. Why not do it?
quote.context: Changelog Interviews #532, Bringing Whisper and LLaMA to the Masses, 2023
